title: X. The Speech For The Defense. An Argument That Cuts Both Ways
paragraphs: A hush fell as the first words of the famous orator rang out. The eyes of the whole audience were fixed on him. He began very simply and directly, with an air of conviction but not the slightest trace of conceit. He made no attempt at eloquence, at pathos or at emotional phrases. He was like a man talking in a circle of close and sympathetic friends. He had a fine voice, deep and sympathetic, and the very sound of it had something genuine and simple about it. Yet everyone realized at once that the speaker might suddenly rise to true pathos and “pierce the heart with untold power.” His language was perhaps less regular than Ippolit Kirillovitch’s. But he did not use long phrases, and in fact he spoke with more precision. One thing displeased the ladies. He kept bending forward, especially at the start. It was not quite bowing; it was as if he were about to dart at his listeners. He folded his long spine nearly in half, as though it had a spring in the middle that let him bend almost to a right angle.

At the start he spoke rather disconnectedly, without system, one might say, taking the facts one at a time, though in the end they added up to a whole. His speech could be divided into two parts. The first was criticism, a refutation of the charge, at times malicious and sarcastic. In the second half, however, he suddenly altered his tone and even his manner, and rose at once to pathos. The audience seemed to have been watching for this, and they quivered with enthusiasm.

He went straight to the point. He began by saying that although he practiced in Petersburg, he had more than once gone to provincial towns to defend prisoners whose innocence he was convinced of, or at least had formed an idea of beforehand. “That is what has happened to me in the present case,” he explained. “From the very first reports in the newspapers, something struck me that strongly disposed me in the prisoner’s favor. What interested me most was a fact that often occurs in legal practice, but rarely, I think, in so extreme and peculiar a form as here. I ought to name that peculiarity only at the end of my speech. But I will name it at the very beginning, for it is my weakness to set to work directly, without keeping my effects in reserve or husbanding my material. That may be imprudent of me, but at least it is sincere. What I have in mind is this. There is an overwhelming chain of evidence against the prisoner, and yet not one fact in it will stand up to criticism when examined on its own. As I followed the case more closely in the papers, this idea grew stronger and stronger. Then I suddenly received a request from the prisoner’s relatives to take up his defense. I hurried here at once, and here I became completely convinced. I undertook the case in order to break down this terrible chain of facts, and to show that each piece of evidence, taken separately, was unproved and fantastic.”

“Gentlemen of the jury,” he suddenly protested, “I am a stranger to this district. I come with no preconceived ideas. The prisoner, a man of turbulent and unbridled temper, has never insulted me. But he has insulted perhaps hundreds of people in this town, and so he has set many of them against him in advance. Of course I recognize that the moral feeling of local society has been justly roused against him. He is a man of violent, turbulent temper. Yet he was received in society here. He was even welcome in the family of my talented friend, the prosecutor.”

(N.B. At these words two or three people laughed in the audience, but they quickly stopped, and everyone noticed. All of us knew that the prosecutor received Mitya against his will, only because Mitya had somehow aroused his wife’s interest. She was a lady of the highest virtue and moral worth, but fanciful, capricious and fond of opposing her husband, especially in trifles. Mitya’s visits, however, had not been frequent.)

“Nevertheless I venture to suggest,” Fetyukovitch continued, “that, for all his independent mind and fair character, my opponent may have formed a mistaken prejudice against my unfortunate client. Oh, that is so natural! The unfortunate man has only too well earned such prejudice. Outraged morality, and still more outraged taste, is often relentless. In the talented prosecutor’s speech we have heard a stern analysis of the prisoner’s character and conduct, and his severe, critical attitude to the case was plain. What is more, he entered into psychological subtleties that he could not have entered if he had felt the slightest conscious and malicious prejudice against the prisoner. But in cases like this there are things even worse, even more fatal, than the most malicious and consciously unfair attitude. It is worse if we are carried away by the artistic instinct, by the desire to create, so to speak, a romance, especially if God has gifted us with psychological insight. Before I set out for this place, I was warned in Petersburg, and I knew myself, that here I should meet a talented opponent whose psychological insight and subtlety had in recent years won him a peculiar fame in legal circles. But profound as psychology is, it is a knife that cuts both ways.” (Laughter among the public.) “You will of course forgive me this comparison. I cannot boast of eloquence. But let me take as an example any point in the prosecutor’s speech.

“The prisoner, running away through the garden in the dark, climbed over the fence. The servant seized him, and he knocked the man down with a brass pestle. Then he jumped back into the garden and spent five minutes over the man, trying to find out whether he had killed him. And the prosecutor refuses to believe the prisoner’s statement that he ran to old Grigory out of pity. ‘No,’ he says, ‘such delicacy of feeling at such a moment is impossible, it is unnatural. He ran to find out whether the only witness of his crime was dead or alive, and so he showed that he had committed the murder, since he would have had no other reason to run back.’

“There you have psychology. But let us take the same method and apply it to the case the other way round, and our result will be no less probable. The murderer, we are told, leapt down to find out, as a precaution, whether the witness was alive. Yet in his murdered father’s study he had left behind, as the prosecutor himself argues, an amazing piece of evidence: a torn envelope with an inscription saying that three thousand roubles had been in it. ‘If he had carried that envelope away with him, no one in the world would have known about the envelope and the notes in it, or that the prisoner had stolen the money.’ Those are the prosecutor’s own words. So on one side you see a complete lack of precaution. Here is a man who has lost his head and fled in a panic, leaving that clue on the floor. Two minutes later, when he has killed another man, we are asked to assume in him the most heartless and calculating foresight. But even granting this, I suppose it is psychological subtlety that discovers that in some circumstances I become as bloodthirsty and sharp-eyed as a Caucasian eagle, while in the next I am as timid and blind as a mole. But if I am so bloodthirsty and so cruelly calculating that, having killed a man, I run back only to see whether he is alive to witness against me, why should I spend five minutes looking after my victim, at the risk of meeting other witnesses? Why soak my handkerchief wiping the blood from his head, so that it can be used as evidence against me later? If he were so cold-hearted and calculating, why not strike the servant again and again on the head with the same pestle, to kill him outright and be rid of all anxiety about the witness?

“Again, though he ran to see whether the witness was alive, he left another witness on the path. That witness was the brass pestle, which he had taken from the two women, and which they could always recognize afterwards as theirs, proving that he had taken it from them. And it is not as if he had forgotten it on the path, or dropped it in carelessness or haste. No, he threw his weapon away, for it was found fifteen paces from where Grigory lay. Why did he do that? Just because he was grieved at having killed a man, an old servant, and so he flung the pestle away with a curse, as a murderous weapon. That is how it must have been. What other reason could he have had for throwing it so far? And if he could feel grief and pity at having killed a man, that shows he was innocent of his father’s murder. Had he murdered his father, he would never have run to another victim out of pity. He would have felt differently. His thoughts would have been centered on saving himself. He would have had none left for pity, and that is beyond doubt. On the contrary, he would have smashed the man’s skull instead of spending five minutes looking after him. There was room for pity and good feeling precisely because his conscience had been clear until then. Here we have a different psychology. I have used this method on purpose, gentlemen of the jury, to show that you can prove anything with it. It all depends on who uses it. Psychology lures even the most serious people into romancing, and quite without their knowing it. I am speaking of the abuse of psychology, gentlemen.”
Sounds of approval and laughter at the prosecutor’s expense were heard again in the court. I will not give the speech in detail. I will quote only some passages from it, some of the leading points.
